This cost is negligible compared to the transform itself [S1].

The claim states that 'This cost is negligible compared to the transform itself'. The evidence explicitly states: 'The encoding of the direction vectors represent a negligible computational cost compared to the other codec components.' While the evidence supports that the cost of *encoding* the direction vectors is negligible, it does not explicitly compare this cost to the cost of the *transform itself* (the exhaustive search and filtering operations). The evidence mentions the time complexity increase of the search (factor of 18 or 9), implying the search/transform cost is significant, but it does not make the specific comparison requested in the claim. Therefore, only part of the claim (negligible cost) is supported, but the specific comparison target ('transform itself') is not explicitly confirmed in the text provided.

**Outputs:** Wavelet coefficients organized into low-pass and high-pass sub-bands; side-information encoding the selected direction vector for each block [S1].

The claim states that the outputs include 'Wavelet coefficients organized into low-pass and high-pass sub-bands' and 'side-information encoding the selected direction vector for each block'. The evidence confirms that the process involves a Directional Adaptive Discrete Wavelet Transform (DA-DWT) which performs an exhaustive search to maximize energy compaction into 'low-pass sub-bands' (implying the existence of high-pass sub-bands as standard in DWT structures). Furthermore, the evidence explicitly mentions that the module 'handles coding the side-information' and that 'the encoding of the direction vectors represent a negligible computational cost', confirming that side-information encoding the selected direction vectors is part of the output process.

The Directional Adaptive Discrete Wavelet Transform (DA-DWT) is a volumetric compression method that selects the optimal wavelet decomposition direction for each data block by exhaustively searching a predefined set of direction vectors to maximize energy compaction into low-pass sub-bands [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the DA-DWT performs an 'exhaustive search' over a 'predefined set of direction vectors' to 'maximize energy compaction into the low-pass sub-bands' and achieve 'transform optimality'. It also confirms that this is a volumetric method (referencing XY-plane and Z-dimensions, and JP3D encoder context). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

The DA-DWT was introduced in the context of wavelet-based volumetric medical image compression, specifically as an enhancement to the JP3D standard [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the DA-DWT is implemented within a codec that handles coding side-information and multiplexes data into a final code-stream, referencing the 'standard JP3D encoder' (Fig. 2) and 'JP3D+DA encoder' (Fig. 3). The text describes the DA-DWT as an enhancement (using exhaustive search for optimality) to the standard wavelet transform process used in this context. The specific details about direction vectors, angle steps, and time complexity factors are all present in the provided notes and passages, confirming the factual basis of the claim.
